First, let's get this straight: High speed rail is very expensive.

Depending on whose figures you believe, the current plan would cost somewhere between 3% and 6% of California's existing GDP. (1) The only reason you should spend this much money (even though a healthy portion of it will be paid for by the federal government) is for a project that fundamentally and substantially improves the state in the long term.
High speed rail has the promise to do this.
Let's back up a little bit.
I've seen a lot of reactions to high speed rail that go along the following lines: I can drive from SF to LA in a few hours and I already own my car, why would I drive to some train station?
And where is the giant parking structure going to go?
And why does the line go through Fresno and Bakersfield and those other blow-away towns?

These initial reactions are mistakes, because high speed rail is not going to serve the California of the past, where roads were wide and open and gas was cheap - the California of the commercials and music videos in which your Impala convertible is the only one visible on the Pacific Coast Highway.
That California - to the extent it ever existed - is gone, and it's not coming back.

In the California of the future, urban highways and busy corridors are congested all the time, and flights are limited by the number of takeoffs and landings in a day. (High speed rail won't change this, either: it's the new normal.) The future California is (and has to be) getting around on something that is not powered by petroleum.
*   It can uniquely accommodate future intra-state transportation demand.
Neither highways nor airplanes are a good choice for moving lots of people along a dense urban corridor.
High speed rail is.
*   It will be the large-scale framework for future development.
The point is those 15 million new people.

If they all live in endless tract subdivisions and hope to get around exclusively in their own cars (even if they're all natural gas, electric, compressed air or whatever), California will find that the effort to build that lifestyle will make things like schools, parks, art, nature, etc. impossible to maintain.
The only hope is to build cities of high value, high touch, reasonably dense neighborhoods where people don't have to drive everywhere.
High speed rail both requires and supports this kind of development.
*   It will support and drive investment in Fresno, Bakersfield and smaller cities.
We already know population will be going disproportionately to these cities; they need to be linked to the state's primary economic drivers.
*   It's really attractive.
It's hard to know how pleasant express train travel can be if you haven't done it.

Trains in Europe and Asia are comfortable and beautiful, run extremely frequently and are almost never late, to the point that many European operators give significant refunds if your train is late - the AVE between Madrid and Seville will refund 100% of your ticket price if your train is more than 5 minutes late. (4) High speed rail on trips of less than three hours typically takes 60% to 100% of market share from airlines.
*   It's utterly established.
I am continually amazed by the discussion of high speed rail in the US that treats it as a sort of crazy utopian idea, or at least highly speculative.
The fact is that high speed rail is a very normal part of transportation infrastructure throughout the world among nations rich and not-that-rich, dense and not-that-dense.
In not having high speed rail, the US is the outlier.
*   It's financially responsible.

High-speed rail is indeed very expensive, but it's also a very long term asset that will provided benefits into the foreseeable future - many key rail corridors are in heavy use over a hundred years after their original creation.
Long term bonds (=requiring future generations to pay for part of the cost) are very appropriate for this kind of development.
Some European and Asian systems are operationally profitable (service is paid for out of fares) and this is a reasonable expectation for California's system.

BOT (Build, Operate, Transfer) is another appropriate model, whereby a private company builds the line with government assistance, operates it for a number of years, and then turns it over to the public.
Taiwan (whose per capital GDP is a fraction of California's) built its system with this model.
The cliche goes "choose the future," which is ridiculous because the future is coming whether you choose it or not.
The choice is whether you want the future to be good or bad - and remember, the choice of "make it all back the way it was supposed to be in 1960" is not on the table.
It's easy to imagine California in 2050 either as the global powerhouse it is today - or as a dusty hellhole, a slum the size of a nation.
I think high speed rail is one of the prerequisites for greatness.

The idea, though, is that once Merced to Palmdale is complete, there will be momentum to complete the rest of the work and establish the necessary shared use agreements with Caltrain in Northern California and Metrolink in Southern California that you'll be able to take a single train from San Francisco to Anaheim by 2029.

That brings us to the larger question: is it dead in reality?
Consider the following.
*   Interstate started construction in 1960 and completed construction in 1979.
*   The Loma Prieta earthquake occurred in 1989, making it very clear that a new east span of the Bay Bridge was necessary.
The new East Span is scheduled to have traffic on it in 2013.
*   Discussions about high speed rail in California began in earnest in 1994.
These sorts of things can take awhile, so it isn't dead.
